subject: horse
name: Catching, Haltering & Turnout (Horse)
summary: The horse's calm willingness and polite personal-space cooperation during approaching, haltering, gate passage, and turnout release.
purpose: Reflects emotional safety around humans, routine predictability, and mutual security at stall doors and turnout gates.
safety: Never mistake tense freeze, shutdown, or learned helplessness (braced muscles, fixed glassy eye, held breath) for genuine relaxed cooperation.

Notice early signs of worry, discomfort, or avoidance—such as pinned ears, high rigid head, or retreating—and investigate pain, gear pinch, or handling stress rather than cornering or escalating pressure.
Prioritize calm space and patience near gates and pasture mates so horses neither crowd handlers nor wheel abruptly at release.

introductory.overview: Permitting comfortable approach in familiar stalls or paddocks, cooperating calmly with haltering, respecting personal space through gates, and waiting settled facing the handler until unclipped at release.

components.title: Genuine comfort vs. shutdown
components.description: Greeting or waiting for approach with soft eye, relaxed breathing, and willing attention rather than braced immobility, defensive ear-pinning, or evading corners.

components.title: Cooperative haltering and personal space
components.description: Accepting touch on neck and poll, lowering or steadying the head calmly into a properly fitted halter without throwing the head up, nibbling, or barging into the handler.

components.title: Calm catching and gate-release routine
components.description: Stepping through familiar stall doors or gates without rushing, turning politely toward the handler/gate, and standing calmly until the halter is lowered clear before walking away.

introductory.learning: Accepts familiar catching, haltering, and turnout with mild hesitation, head-raising, crowding through the doorway, or pulling away slightly before the halter is fully released.
introductory.proficient: Calmly accepts approach and haltering in familiar spaces with genuine relaxed expression, respects personal-space boundaries through doorways and gates, and waits settled until calmly unclipped before turning away.

intermediate.overview: Maintaining comfortable haltering, polite gate spacing, and emotional steadiness across larger pastures, herd-mate interactions, energetic weather, or unfamiliar venues.

components.title: Confidence around herd dynamics and varied routines
components.description: Leaving or rejoining pasture companions safely without pushing into the handler, striking, kicking near gates, or bolting explosively once released.

components.title: Stress recognition and calm recovery
components.description: Expressing mild curiosity or alertness appropriately while settling calmly back into relaxed attention on light handler cues even when herd members call or run nearby.

intermediate.learning: Maintains composure in group pastures or novel settings with occasional restlessness near herd mates, distracted scanning, or hurried steps immediately after gate passage.
intermediate.proficient: Demonstrates consistent confidence and polite personal-space respect during catching, haltering, gate transit, and turnout across larger pastures, herd groups, or energetic days without barging, bolting, or anxious shutdown.

exercises.title: Relaxed Greeting, Haltering, and Gate Wait
exercises.summary: In a familiar stall or paddock, give the horse time to greet easily as you approach the shoulder, lower or soften its head comfortably for haltering, walk smoothly through the gate without crowding, and pause facing you quietly before unclipping at release.
exercises.whatToNotice: Look for soft blinking, relaxed ears, and settled stillness during unclipping rather than pinned ears, raised tension, or wheeling away the instant the gate opens.

exercises.title: Composed Catching and Turnout Around Herd Mates
exercises.summary: Practice polite haltering, roomy gate spacing, and steady release in larger pastures or lively weather with companions nearby, rewarding the horse for maintaining soft attention and polite personal space rather than dashing off.
exercises.whatToNotice: Observe whether curiosity about herd mates stays manageable—can the horse glance at friends and settle smoothly back onto your cue?

commonDifficulties.issue: Spinning and bolting the moment the halter slips off
commonDifficulties.guidance: Rushing off often builds from anticipation or gate crowding. Walk farther into the paddock, pause facing the gate, offer a gentle scratch, and slip the halter smoothly only once feet stay settled.

commonDifficulties.issue: Walking away repeatedly when approached in pasture
commonDifficulties.guidance: Avoidance can reflect uncomfortable work, ear sensitivity, or past chasing. Visit peacefully without demanding work every time and assess physical comfort if avoidance appeared suddenly.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: How a horse leaves you at turnout reveals how comfortable they felt during the time they just spent with you.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Do not mistake a frozen, glassy-eyed horse standing rigid in a corner for happy cooperation; watch breathing, muscle ease, and social pressure from pasture mates.

subject: horse
name: Leading & Halter Response
summary: The horse's ability to yield politely to light halter requests and lead calmly beside a handler.
purpose: Forms the foundation for safe daily handling, veterinary/farrier care, and groundwork.
safety: Introduce halter requests in calm, enclosed spaces before expecting steady poise near busy distractions.
Check halter fit, poll/noseband comfort, and dental ease before assuming pulling or head-shyness is behavioral defiance.

introductory.overview: Yielding willingly to light halter requests (forward, halt, calm step back, turns) and matching walk pace beside the handler in familiar settings.

components.title: Halter softness and personal space
components.description: Shifting weight smoothly off light halter requests without bracing through the poll, leaning on the handler, or crowding personal space.

components.title: Relaxed walk matching
components.description: Walking beside the handler on a softly draped lead in steady four-beat rhythm—waiting calmly at halts rather than fidgeting.

introductory.learning: Leads and yields in quiet areas with occasional pushing into the handler's space, lagging, or head tossing when asked to check pace.
introductory.proficient: Calmly and reliably yields to light halter requests and leads attentively at walk on a relaxed lead without crowding, dragging, or bolting in familiar spaces.

intermediate.overview: Leading calmly through walk, trot-up, transitions, and narrow spaces while remaining composed around outdoor or herd distractions.

components.title: Trot transitions and busy-setting composure
components.description: Stepping into an active straight trot beside the handler on light invitation, halting squarely without leaning, and staying focused when other horses or activity move nearby.

intermediate.learning: Leads at trot or in novel environments with intermittent rushing, distraction pulling, or surging ahead during transitions.
intermediate.proficient: Consistently leads calmly at walk and trot on a light lead across varied or busy settings, matching pace transitions promptly while honoring personal space.

exercises.title: Soft Feel, Polite Spacing, and Settled Halts
exercises.summary: In a familiar enclosure, invite the horse to yield softly at the poll and step smoothly into a relaxed four-beat walk, match pauses without drifting past the handler, and offer a polite backward step if personal space narrows. Allow brief, unpressured pauses so light halter cues remain predictable.
exercises.whatToNotice: Look for a supple jaw, even walking footfalls on a loose lead, and settled pauses without crowding, rubbing on you, or leaning into the halter.

exercises.title: Steady Poise Past Everyday Activity
exercises.summary: Lead along open paths through balanced turns, brief pauses, and—where space, footing, and soundness permit—a straight, even trot-up near mild barn activity while maintaining respectful spacing.
exercises.whatToNotice: Does the horse stay balanced through the shoulders and attentive to light requests near gentle distractions, rather than surging ahead, lagging behind, or bracing tightly?

commonDifficulties.issue: Leaning into or bracing against halter pressure
commonDifficulties.guidance: Pressing back usually reflects confusion or discomfort rather than stubbornness. Simplify to smaller requests, release on the earliest weight shift, and verify noseband and poll comfort.

commonDifficulties.issue: Crowding into space or scattering attention
commonDifficulties.guidance: Over-stimulation or unclear boundaries pull focus away. Return briefly to lower-distraction footing, keep boundaries consistent, and give curiosity room to settle without scolding.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: A horse that trusts light halter communication carries that steadiness into veterinary care, trailering, and work under saddle.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Distinguish genuine settling—soft eye, regular breathing, slack jaw—from anxious freezing with a raised head; check poll fit, teeth, or hooves if head-shyness or trot reluctance appears.

subject: horse
name: Standing Quietly
summary: The horse's ability to stand calmly and patiently when tied, held, or asked to wait in place.
purpose: Keeps the horse safe and relaxed during grooming, tacking, waiting at trailers, and farrier or vet visits.
safety: Always tie with safe hardware and breakaway/quick-release setups; never ask a horse to ground-tie near traffic or unenclosed hazards.
Look for true relaxation (soft eye, quiet breathing, lower neck/lip) rather than mistaking tense shutdown or freeze for calm standing.

introductory.overview: Standing calmly with genuine relaxation—not tight freeze tension—when tied safely or held in a familiar spot.

components.title: Relaxed standing vs. freeze tension
components.description: Settling calmly for routine grooming or care without pulling back, pawing, or crowding—showing soft breathing and alert-but-easy posture rather than brittle stillness before a spook.

introductory.learning: Stands tied for short periods with occasional shifting, pawing, or tight anxious posture.
introductory.proficient: Stands quietly with relaxed breathing and soft posture when tied or held in familiar settings for routine care without pulling back, pawing, or crowding.

intermediate.overview: Maintaining calm composure while tied at trailers, wash areas, or busier venues—even when herd mates step away.

components.title: Emotional regulation around commotion
components.description: Staying settled when neighboring horses walk past, vehicles move, or unfamiliar sights occur nearby—recovering calmly after mild startles.

intermediate.learning: Stands in busier environments with intermittent fidgeting, calling, or leaning back against the lead.
intermediate.proficient: Stands calmly and reliably when tied or held in unfamiliar or lively settings—including trailers and group venues—without panicking, pawing excessively, or pulling back.

advanced.overview: Settling calmly in place on a dropped or completely slack line (ground-tying) in safe enclosed or appropriate settings.

components.title: Composed ground-tie patience
components.description: Waiting steadily in position while the handler steps away and moves calmly around, remaining relaxed without grazing, wandering, or anxious spinning.

advanced.learning: Waits with lead dropped briefly in quiet arenas before wandering toward grass, gates, or other horses.
advanced.proficient: Reliably stands calmly in place on a dropped lead in safe settings while the handler steps away and returns, without wandering, grazing, or fussing.

exercises.title: Genuine Relaxation While Held or Safely Tied
exercises.summary: In a familiar spot with a safe breakaway or quick-release setup, ask the horse to wait for brief, comfortable intervals while you groom or stand nearby—ending each wait while breathing stays soft rather than waiting for restlessness.
exercises.whatToNotice: Watch for a resting hip, soft eye, regular breathing, and lowered neck tension rather than rigid frozen stillness or pawing.

exercises.title: Composure at Busy Venues and Optional Ground-Tying
exercises.summary: Gradually expose the horse to brief waits near wash areas, trailers, or when a companion steps away—and for advanced horses in enclosed, hazard-free spaces only, introduce settling in place on a draped lead before returning to reward.
exercises.whatToNotice: Observe how smoothly the horse settles back after a passing sound or departing barn mate without pulling against the tie or pacing tightly.

commonDifficulties.issue: Pawing or fidgeting persistently while tied
commonDifficulties.guidance: Restlessness often stems from boredom, hunger, isolation stress, or waiting too long. Shorten wait sessions, confirm forage or companion comfort nearby, and reward moments of settled standing.

commonDifficulties.issue: Pulling back sharply when feeling rope tension
commonDifficulties.guidance: Panic against fixed resistance escalates dangerously. Always use breakaway hardware, teach soft poll yielding in hand first, and never leave a worried pull-back horse tied unattended.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: True patience is a relaxed mind and soft breath—never a tight horse holding its breath waiting for permission to flee.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Always use safe breakaway setups, avoid tying horses alone for long stretches without forage or water, and never practice ground-tying near roads, open gates, or hazards.

subject: horse
name: Daily Care Handling
summary: The horse's calm cooperation during routine care—grooming, blanketing, bathing, and tacking up.
purpose: Reduces stress and injury risk during everyday care and preparation.
safety: Build comfort gradually with positive timing; never overpower sensitivity around ears, girth, or flanks through harsh restraint.
Always assess physical comfort—recurring girthy biting, ear pinning, or flinching along the back often indicates ulcers, skin irritation, or poorly fitting tack.

introductory.overview: Cooperating calmly for routine grooming, blanketing, gentle sponge or leg water rinsing, and familiar tacking/bridling.

components.title: Calm grooming, blanketing, and mild water
components.description: Accepting brushes, blankets, chest/leg straps, and gentle wet-sponge wiping or lower-leg rinsing calmly without biting, kicking, or bracing away.

components.title: Considerate tacking acceptance and welfare signals
components.description: Standing peacefully while clean pads, saddle, girth/cinch, and bridle are placed; mild ear or girth sensitivity should prompt handlers to check fit and pain early.

introductory.learning: Accepts grooming, blanketing, mild water, and tacking with brief ear pinning, shifting away from the girth, or head raising.
introductory.proficient: Cooperates calmly for routine grooming, blanketing, gentle sponge or lower-leg water care, and familiar saddling and bridling without biting, kicking, or sustained bracing.

intermediate.overview: Remaining relaxed through full-body bathing/hosing, sprays or clippers, and preparation in busy clinics, wash bays, or unfamiliar venues.

components.title: Full bathing and sensory adaptability
components.description: Staying settled through full-body hose rinsing, scraping, fly sprays, body-clipping noise, and tacking up smoothly amid busy unfamiliar sights.

intermediate.learning: Accepts full hosing, sprays, or busy prep spaces with occasional fidgeting, tail clamping, or head tossing.
intermediate.proficient: Remains calm and cooperative during full-body bathing, routine sprays or clippers, blanketing, and tacking across unfamiliar or lively venues.

exercises.title: Relaxed Touch Across Sensitive Care Zones
exercises.summary: During everyday grooming, blanketing, gentle leg rinsing, and familiar tacking, pause and soften whenever the horse shows relaxed acceptance near ears, chest, belly, or saddle area so care feels predictable rather than rushed.
exercises.whatToNotice: Look for soft lips, relaxed tail, and even weight across all four legs rather than tucked flanks, swishing, or bracing as the girth or bridle approaches.

exercises.title: Steady Cooperation for Bathing, Sprays, and New Spaces
exercises.summary: Introduce full hosing, fly sprays, clippers, or tacking in busier wash bays gradually—starting at neutral shoulder areas at low intensity and pausing immediately when tension drops rather than forcing through panic.
exercises.whatToNotice: Notice whether muscle tension softens within a few seconds of pausing—if stress climbs steadily, step back to an easier distance or lighter tool.

commonDifficulties.issue: Ears pinning or snapping when the girth or saddle appears
commonDifficulties.guidance: Girthiness is one of the clearest physical comfort signals horses offer. Rule out saddle pinch, gastric discomfort, or rushing the cinch before treating it as a training issue.

commonDifficulties.issue: Flinching away from sprays or buzzing clippers
commonDifficulties.guidance: Spraying straight into a worried horse’s flank builds avoidance. Spray onto a cloth first or introduce gentle sound at a distance where curiosity stays intact.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: Cooperative care grows from hundreds of small moments where your horse learns that relaxing makes rushing stop.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Never overpower ear, mouth, or belly sensitivity with harsh restraint; persistent defensive behavior during routine care warrants checking tack fit, skin, teeth, and digestive comfort.

subject: horse
name: Hoof Handling
summary: The horse's ability to yield all four hooves willingly, balance calmly, and cooperate for hoof cleaning and farrier care.
purpose: Essential for safe daily hoof maintenance and stress-free trimming or shoeing.
safety: Honor the horse's physical balance and joint comfort—older, sore, or stiff horses need time to shift weight onto remaining legs before lifting a hoof.

introductory.overview: Shifting balance calmly and lifting each hoof willingly on light cue for comfortable routine cleaning.

components.title: Balanced lifting and comfort signals
components.description: Transferring weight smoothly without throwing itself off balance, holding each foot calmly for picking, and setting it down gently—noting that sudden snatching often indicates joint pain, imbalance, or thrush discomfort.

introductory.learning: Yields hooves with hesitation, leaning heavily onto the handler, or snatching a foot back prematurely.
introductory.proficient: Shifts weight comfortably, yields all four hooves willingly on light cue, and holds each calmly for routine hoof cleaning without snatching or leaning heavily.

intermediate.overview: Holding posture calmly and cooperatively through complete farrier trimming, rasping, hoof-stand rest, or shoeing on all four hooves.

components.title: Farrier stillness and tool composure
components.description: Remaining relaxed around hoof stands, rasp vibration, nippers, or unfamiliar farriers across longer intervals.

intermediate.learning: Cooperates for short trimming segments before growing restless, leaning, or trying to pull away.
intermediate.proficient: Stands calmly and cooperates comfortably through complete farrier trimming or shoeing sessions on all four hooves.

exercises.title: Balanced Weight Shift and Willing Hoof Lift
exercises.summary: Standing on level non-slip footing, encourage the horse gently to shift weight onto the supporting legs before lifting a hoof just to comfortable height for a few settled seconds, setting it down smoothly before balance wobbles or the foot snatches back.
exercises.whatToNotice: Watch whether the horse organizes balance easily onto the remaining three legs and yields the hoof softly without leaning heavily on your shoulder.

exercises.title: Farrier-Ready Stamina and Comfortable Hoof Rest
exercises.summary: Build comfortable holding duration gradually across all four feet, including gentle tapping on the hoof wall or resting forward on a hoof stand so full trimming and rasping sessions stay predictable and comfortable.
exercises.whatToNotice: Check for uneven stiffness between left and right sides or front and hind limbs—holding a stiff hock too high or too far back triggers understandable resistance.

commonDifficulties.issue: Snatching a hoof back abruptly mid-cleaning
commonDifficulties.guidance: Snatching frequently signals lost balance, joint stiffness, or holding too high. Lower the hoof slightly, keep holds brief, and return the foot smoothly once the leg relaxes.

commonDifficulties.issue: Leaning all body weight onto the handler
commonDifficulties.guidance: Leaning makes picking feet exhausting and unsafe. Pause before lifting, invite a small shift onto the opposite leg first, and check older or stiff horses for joint discomfort.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: Set the foot down while your horse is still balanced and comfortable, and they will hold it willingly far longer next time.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Respect joint range of motion—senior, arthritic, or stiff horses often need lower hoof height, soft footing, and short breaks during trimming.

subject: horse
name: Veterinary & Medical Handling
summary: The horse's calm cooperation during health checks, vital-sign measurement, oral medication, and routine veterinary examinations.
purpose: Allows accurate vital signs, safe treatment, and calmer emergency care.
safety: Condition medical touch gradually when the horse is healthy and relaxed—waiting until an urgent injury makes exam stress much harder.
Respect real pain guarding around injuries, eyes, or abdomen rather than escalating pressure.

intermediate.overview: Standing calmly for unfamiliar veterinary handlers, full TPR vital measurements, routine exam procedures, and smooth oral syringe dosing.

components.title: Unfamiliar handlers, vitals, and oral dosing
components.description: Remaining cooperative when a veterinarian or technician checks temperature, heart/lung sounds, limbs, and oral medication syringes without bolting, striking, or throwing the head violently.

intermediate.learning: Tolerates unfamiliar veterinary checks or oral syringes with mild tension, clamped tail, or tossing head.
intermediate.proficient: Stands calmly and cooperatively with unfamiliar handlers for thorough physical exams, temperature/pulse/respiration measurement, and calm oral medication without panic or evasion.

introductory.overview: Calmly accepting familiar-handler wellness handling—ears, eyes, gums, skin check, stethoscope contact, tail lift, and light limb palpation.

components.title: Familiar-handler health-check cooperation
components.description: Standing softly while a known handler checks eyes, parts lips calmly to inspect gums, lifts the tail briefly, glides hands along legs and belly, and rests a cool stethoscope against ribs without flinching or pulling away.

introductory.learning: Permits familiar-handler eye, mouth, leg, or tail checks for brief moments with mild head-shyness or shifting.
introductory.proficient: Calmly accepts familiar-handler routine wellness handling—eye/lip/gum checks, limb palpation, stethoscope contact, and brief tail lifting—with relaxed posture and no panic.

exercises.title: Relaxed Wellness Touch on Healthy Days
exercises.summary: When the horse is completely healthy and settled, practice brief handling of ears, eyelids, gums, tail lift, flanks, and lower limbs—plus resting a cool spoon or stethoscope lightly behind the elbow—ending each brief touch with rest.
exercises.whatToNotice: Observe whether breathing stays steady and the jaw remains soft as each area is touched, spotting sensitive zones long before an urgent exam.

exercises.title: Unfamiliar-Handler Exams and Easy Oral Dosing
exercises.summary: Practice settled standing while a familiar helper mimics unfamiliar veterinary routines—listening to gut quadrants, checking digital pulses, lifting the tail for thermometer prep, or offering benign oral syringe taste rehearsals on an empty mouth.
exercises.whatToNotice: Notice how rapidly the horse settles when a second person stands beside the shoulder—predictable routines cut emergency clinic stress dramatically.

commonDifficulties.issue: Clamping the tail tightly or dancing away from hind checks
commonDifficulties.guidance: Surprise touch near the hindquarters feels threatening. Announce softly at the hip first, touch briefly and withdraw before tension spikes, and keep positioning safe.

commonDifficulties.issue: Resisting handling only when genuinely hurt or colicky
commonDifficulties.guidance: Pain guarding around eyes, wounds, or abdomen is protective, not defiant. Respect discomfort and let your veterinarian guide safe handling or sedation when needed.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: The best time to teach your horse to trust a thermometer, stethoscope, and syringe is on an ordinary healthy Tuesday.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Never escalate force against pain guarding; cooperative preparation lowers stress, while real medical pain always deserves gentle veterinary care.

subject: horse
name: In-Hand Obstacles & Outings (Horse)
summary: The horse's calm curiosity, footwork coordination, and emotional recovery when investigating unfamiliar ground features, objects, and outdoor environments in-hand.
purpose: Builds resilient confidence and problem-solving trust alongside a handler before encountering new footing, sights, or trails under saddle.
safety: Give the horse clear time to look, sniff, and process unfamiliar surfaces or objects—never flood or drag a worried horse forcefully into panic.
Check footing traction, sharp hazards, overhead clearance, and surface stability before inviting the horse forward.
Respect personal space during moments of startle; reward calm curiosity and quiet recovery rather than demanding rushed crossing.

introductory.overview: Investigating simple, safe unfamiliar objects or ground features and quiet property paths calmly—stepping through with unhurried footwork and recovering steadily after brief hesitation without needing specific competition props.

components.title: Willing investigation without forced exposure
components.description: Lowering the head politely to sniff or inspect harmless unfamiliar objects, ground surface changes, or quiet paths rather than freezing rigidly or spinning away immediately.

components.title: Thoughtful footwork and coordination
components.description: Stepping over or across simple ground features calmly in balanced walk rhythm without leaping frantically or crowding into the handler's space.

components.title: Calm recovery from uncertainty
components.description: Accepting reassurance and settling breathing promptly back into relaxed walking after encountering mild surprises.

introductory.learning: Investigates simple objects or quiet property lanes with brief snorting, stopping, hurried exit steps, or mild drifting near the handler.
introductory.proficient: Investigates simple unfamiliar ground features, everyday novel objects, and quiet paths calmly on a light lead—stepping smoothly in balance without rushing, bolting, or crowding, and settling quickly after minor uncertainty. No specific competition obstacles are required.

intermediate.overview: Demonstrating adaptable confidence, balanced footing coordination, and reliable composure across varied outdoor trails, uneven ground, unfamiliar venues, or everyday distractions on the ground.

components.title: Confidence across unfamiliar environments
components.description: Remaining curious, polite, and attentive to light handler guidance while hand-walking near varied trail surfaces, modest slopes, breezy objects, passing walkers/cyclists, or busy venue outskirts.

components.title: Balance, coordination, and steady recovery
components.description: Adjusting foot placement deliberately over uneven natural terrain or suitable ground obstacles without panicking, and regaining calm composure rapidly if momentarily startled.

intermediate.learning: Handles varied outdoor outings and natural surfaces with occasional watchful tension, surged forward steps past noises, or crowding when passing distractions.
intermediate.proficient: Navigates varied ground environments, natural terrain changes, and unfamiliar outdoor settings calmly in-hand—balancing sure-footedly, honoring personal space, and recovering smoothly from unexpected distractions without forced exposure.

exercises.title: Open Curiosity Around Simple Ground Features
exercises.summary: On safe, flat ground, let the horse approach a single pole, low mat, or quiet barn lane at an easy pace, lower its neck to inspect and sniff, and step through smoothly at walk with thoughtful foot placement.
exercises.whatToNotice: Look for ears turning forward with curiosity, head lowering to judge footing, and measured stepping rather than leaping high or rushing past.

exercises.title: Adaptable Footwork and Recovery Outside the Arena
exercises.summary: Explore gentle outdoor paths, mild terrain slopes, or unfamiliar safe ground features while allowing pauses to process passing sounds or sights, rewarding quick return to loose breathing and even footwork.
exercises.whatToNotice: Observe how rapidly breathing and muscle tension settle after a brief look—steady recovery matters far more than pretending nothing ever startles a horse.

commonDifficulties.issue: Planting feet and staring rigidly at an unfamiliar surface
commonDifficulties.guidance: Freezing is a horse gathering information. Give a brief pause without pulling on the halter, let the horse inspect at an easier distance, and reward the first relaxed step forward.

commonDifficulties.issue: Bolting past the object once halfway across
commonDifficulties.guidance: Rushing off signals lingering worry. Pause once clear, let breathing drop, and make the next approach simpler and wider rather than repeating rapidly.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: A confident horse is not one that never looks—it is one that can look, breathe, think, and place its feet safely.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Never drag or flood a frightened horse across an unstable surface; verify traction and overhead clearance first and respect personal space if a startle occurs.

subject: horse
name: Trailer Loading
summary: The horse's willingness to walk calmly into a trailer, wait quietly while secured, and unload smoothly without rushing.
purpose: Supports safe, low-stress transport for travel, outings, and emergencies.
safety: Allow calm sniff-and-process pauses at the threshold; rushing or crowding raises panic and teaches horses to bolt backward at full speed.

intermediate.overview: Walking calmly into unfamiliar or closed-style trailers, waiting patiently while dividers/butt bars/doors close, and unloading safely step by step.

components.title: Closing composure and step-by-step unload
components.description: Remaining settled while butt bars and doors fasten before tying (waiting patiently rather than banging or leaning back against restraints) and stepping calmly out only when asked.

intermediate.learning: Loads in varied trailers or waits for securing with occasional restlessness, pawing, or crowding the exit before release.
intermediate.proficient: Walks calmly into familiar or unfamiliar trailers on light request, waits quietly while dividers and rear doors are secured, stays relaxed when tied, and unloads smoothly at a controlled walk.

introductory.overview: Investigating calmly, stepping onto the ramp or step-up into a safe, open, familiar parked trailer, pausing quietly, and exiting calmly on request.

components.title: Confident exploration and calm threshold entry
components.description: Dropping the head to assess footing willingly, walking smoothly into an open familiar trailer without lunging forward, standing quietly inside for a moment, and stepping or backing out smoothly without explosive bolting.

introductory.learning: Inspects and steps part or all of the way into an open trailer with hesitation, stopping halfway, or hurried exit steps.
introductory.proficient: Calmly investigates and walks into an open, parked trailer on light invitation, pauses quietly inside on a relaxed line, and steps out smoothly at walk without panicking or rushing.

exercises.title: Relaxed Threshold Inspection and First Steps
exercises.summary: With a hitched, bright, open trailer on flat ground, allow the horse to sniff the ramp or step-up without crowding, step one or two hooves smoothly onto the entry, pause peacefully to breathe, and step neatly back off on cue before asking further.
exercises.whatToNotice: Watch for a lowered neck, deliberate step placement, and settled stillness on the ramp rather than wide eyes, rushed plunging forward, or flying backward.

exercises.title: Settled Waiting Inside and Measured Unloading
exercises.summary: Build toward walking evenly all the way inside, standing relaxed while dividers and rear barriers settle safely, and stepping down on request one careful stride at a time without rushing the ramp or step-up.
exercises.whatToNotice: Observe whether the horse breathes evenly inside the stall and waits for a soft exit cue rather than backing out explosively as soon as the barrier opens.

commonDifficulties.issue: Scrambling backward rapidly off the ramp
commonDifficulties.guidance: Fast backing comes from feeling trapped. Practice asking gently for one small backward step before the horse panics, keeping loading sessions short and ending on relaxed stillness.

commonDifficulties.issue: Entering willingly but growing anxious when doors close
commonDifficulties.guidance: Claustrophobia responds best to tiny increments—spend quiet time standing inside with doors open and hay available before closing dividers gradually with a calm helper.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: When a horse discovers the trailer is a safe place to pause and rest, loading stops feeling like a battle.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Rushing, shouting, or crowding a worried horse into a trailer creates lasting loading trauma and serious loading injury risks; slow down or enlist skilled in-person help.

subject: horse
name: Longeing (In-Hand)
summary: The horse's calm comprehension, balance, responsiveness, and willing participation when guided on a longe line.
purpose: Develops attentive voice/body responsiveness, balanced curved movement without a rider's weight, and calm confidence on a light line.
safety: Work on level, non-slip footing with generous joint-protecting circle sizes—especially for young, green, stiff, or large-framed horses.
Never require faster gaits merely to prove higher proficiency; respect conditioning, soundness, and mental readiness at every level.
Distinguish relaxed attentiveness from frantic circling, defensive pulling, or anxious shutdown—investigate persistent one-sided reluctance or head tilting for discomfort.

introductory.overview: Calmly understanding light ground cues to step out onto a respectful working distance, move settled in both directions at a comfortable pace (such as walk), halt, and step inward politely on invitation—without crowding or fleeing. Faster gaits such as trot or canter are not required.

components.title: Understanding light circle and pause cues
components.description: Stepping calmly out onto a line on gentle sending requests, turning cleanly without tangling, and halting settled on the circle or approaching politely when invited in.

components.title: Maintaining a respectful working distance
components.description: Holding comfortable spacing outward along the arc without drifting onto the handler's toes or lunging tightly outward against the halter/cavesson.

components.title: Willingness and emotional composure
components.description: Participating with soft jaw, ear awareness, and steady breathing rather than bolting out of worry or shutting down reluctantly.

introductory.learning: Steps onto a circle in familiar enclosed footing while occasionally drifting inward, pulling steadily outward, turning to face abruptly, or hesitating on transitions between left and right directions.
introductory.proficient: Calmly understands light longeing requests in both directions at a comfortable pace (such as walk), maintains a respectful working distance without leaning or bolting, settles into halt, and yields inward politely on invitation. Faster gaits are not required.

intermediate.overview: Showing developing coordination, steady rhythm, light non-pulling line communication, and responsive direction or pace transitions suited to horse readiness and footing—without mandating canter.

components.title: Transition and direction responsiveness
components.description: Responding smoothly on light posture, line, and voice cues across walk and appropriate pace changes suited to age and fitness (trot where comfortable; canter remaining optional), plus calm reverse transitions without confusion.

components.title: Developing balance and bilateral symmetry
components.description: Beginning to balance smoothly through the shoulder and ribcage on generous circles in both directions rather than bracing outward or falling heavily inward.

components.title: Composure and comfort awareness
components.description: Remaining relaxed and attentive around minor ambient distractions while showing honest ease through back and limbs.

intermediate.learning: Works smoothly across comfortable circle transitions in one direction while occasionally rushing, losing circle distance around distractions, or leaning slightly inward on the stiffer side.
intermediate.proficient: Responds willingly on a light line in both directions across walk and appropriate pace transitions suited to its fitness (without requiring canter), maintains consistent distance and improving symmetry, and stays relaxed and attentive around routine distractions.

advanced.overview: Demonstrating poised balance, subtle cue responsiveness, within-gait adaptability, and willing adjustment across varied circle paths or requests—prioritizing relaxation and sound comfort over speed or specific obstacle props.

components.title: Subtle responsiveness and comfortable self-carriage
components.description: Answering quiet voice, breath, and light line cues with relaxed, carrying balance suited to conformation—adjusting stride length, tempo, or posture smoothly without bracing.

components.title: Adaptability across tracks and requests
components.description: Following varied circle sizes, gentle spirals, or moving ovals/tracks across the arena willingly while staying composed through any optional gymnastic exercises—never requiring faster speed or poles as fixed tests.

advanced.learning: Follows subtle stride or track changes well in familiar spaces while occasionally stiffening briefly during smaller spirals or quicker tempo adjustments.
advanced.proficient: Responds softly to minimal longeing cues in both directions—adapting stride, balance suited to its build, and varied paths (such as spirals or moving circles) willingly with relaxed composure across diverse requests.

exercises.title: Level Arcs at a Settled Walk
exercises.summary: On level, non-slip footing, ask the horse smoothly onto a wide working circle at walk in both directions while keeping clear of hindquarters kicking reach. Ask for a settled halt out on the arc before inviting the horse politely inward to rest—without requiring faster gaits.
exercises.whatToNotice: Look for a relaxed line drape, regular breathing, and loose shoulders carrying an even curve, rather than leaning hard outward, drifting in, or turning defensively.

exercises.title: Symmetric Balance Across Changing Tracks
exercises.summary: Along wide circles and shifting ovals in both directions, encourage smooth transitions between walk, halt, and any faster gait suited to age, fitness, and footing—changing rein regularly so both sides develop evenly.
exercises.whatToNotice: Notice whether the inside shoulder lifts lightly and the ribcage bends similarly in both directions, or if one rein brings rushing, falling inward, or a tilted head.

commonDifficulties.issue: Accelerating or pulling steadily outward on the line
commonDifficulties.guidance: Tight curves or sharp driving posture often overwhelm balance. Enlarge the track into open arena space, settle back to walk, and reward relaxed rhythm with rest.

commonDifficulties.issue: Turning abruptly to face or stalling mid-circle
commonDifficulties.guidance: Confusing body angles, overlong bouts, or early fatigue often trigger abrupt stops. Keep sessions brief, clarify personal space when pausing, and simplify the question before increasing pressure.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: Good longeing builds relaxed understanding and curved balance—never endurance fatigue or fast, tight circling.
learningGuide.welfareNote: A quieter response may indicate true relaxation, but always read posture and breathing to rule out anxious shutdown. Keep arcs wide, footing sound, sessions brief, and investigate one-sided stiffness for soreness.

subject: horse
name: Ground Driving
summary: The horse's learned ability to move forward, halt, and turn calmly in response to two long lines handled from behind or beside it.
purpose: Builds confidence, steering clarity, and forward acceptance without a rider's weight.
safety: Ensure calm desensitization to lines brushing legs/quarters before driving solo, and rule out mouth, poll, or back soreness if the horse braces sharply.

introductory.overview: Accepting surcingle and long lines comfortably along sides and hips, stepping forward calmly, and halting/turning in an enclosed area.

components.title: Relaxed line acceptance vs. freeze
components.description: Moving forward softly without clenching the back, clamping the tail, or locking up when two long lines lightly touch sides or hindquarters.

components.title: Soft walk, halt, and basic turns
components.description: Responding calmly to light steering and halt requests without diving toward the handler or rushing forward.

introductory.learning: Accepts driving gear and lines with brief stiffness or hesitation; may halt abruptly or turn inward toward the handler.
introductory.proficient: Calmly accepts long-lining equipment and lines touching sides and legs, walks forward confidently, and halts and turns both ways in an enclosed space on light requests.

intermediate.overview: Working forward smoothly at walk and trot on long lines with balanced alignment, prompt transitions, and composure in varied spaces.

components.title: Trot balance, straightness, and line composure
components.description: Holding straight tracks, clean turns, and prompt walk–trot transitions while staying relaxed if lines touch hocks unexpectedly.

intermediate.learning: Works at trot or varied venues with occasional rushing, leaning against one line, or crookedness through turns.
intermediate.proficient: Moves forward confidently at walk and trot in steady rhythm and straightness, completes prompt transitions and clean turns on light requests, and stays composed across varied settings.

exercises.title: Relaxed Acceptance of Surcingle and Lines
exercises.summary: With a confident handler in an enclosed arena—and an experienced helper for early sessions—let the horse grow comfortable wearing a padded surcingle and feeling soft lines brush along flanks and hips before walking smoothly forward, halting, and making wide turns.
exercises.whatToNotice: Look for loose tail carriage, steady walking rhythm, and relaxed acceptance when lines brush lightly against the hindquarters rather than clamping down or kicking out.

exercises.title: Aligned Walk and Trot Steering on Two Lines
exercises.summary: Once line acceptance and walk turns feel natural, build balanced straight lines, wide circles, and smooth walk-to-halt or walk-to-trot transitions on light, even feel across varied safe arena patterns.
exercises.whatToNotice: Observe whether the horse bends softly through the ribs on turns and accepts light half-halts without bracing behind the bit or rushing ahead.

commonDifficulties.issue: Tucking the tail tightly or kicking when a line touches a leg
commonDifficulties.guidance: Unexpected hind-leg contact triggers startle reflexes. Step back to stationary line desensitization with a helper until the horse stays completely loose before walking on.

commonDifficulties.issue: Rushing forward or ducking sharply on turns
commonDifficulties.guidance: Sudden speed signals confusion or heavy rein feel. Simplify back to straight walk-halt clarity on an open line and verify bit, halter, and surcingle fit.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: Comfortable acceptance of lines around the hindquarters comes first; steering and transitions grow easily once the horse trusts the gear.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Do not rush solo driving on an unprepared horse, verify comfortable padded surcingle wither clearance, and check poll, mouth, or back comfort if sharp bracing appears.

subject: horse
name: Yielding the Hindquarters (In-Hand)
summary: The horse's calm comprehension, emotional composure, and coordinated hindquarter crossing when asked from the ground to step its hips aside around steadier shoulders.
purpose: Builds respectful personal space, calmness during gating, saddling, and care routines, hindquarter balance awareness, and clear groundwork readiness for mounted lateral cues.
safety: Distinguish calm understanding from flinging the hips in fear, spinning to escape, kicking out, or shutting down under excessive pressure.
Practice on level, non-slip footing and allow the horse to pause and settle promptly upon offering a calm crossing response.
Repeated one-sided bracing, tail-wringing, or reluctance to cross behind can indicate hip, stifle, hock, or back discomfort—evaluate comfort before repeating asks.

introductory.overview: From halt or a quiet pause, calmly understanding light ground requests in both directions to step the hindquarters aside around relatively steady shoulders and settle softly on release—without flight, spinning, or bracing.

components.title: Calm understanding vs. escape
components.description: Stepping smoothly with soft eye, jaw, and breathing rather than whipping the hips away in alarm, pinning ears, or freezing.

components.title: Developing crossing coordination and pause
components.description: Stepping the inside hind leg comfortably across in front of the outside hind without tangling or rushing, then pausing settled when pressure releases.

introductory.learning: Responds in familiar settings with brief hesitation, crowding, forward or backward drift, hurried steps on one side, or mild tension before settling.
introductory.proficient: Calmly understands light ground cues from halt to step its hindquarters aside cleanly in both directions with soft expression, comfortable posture, and balanced crossing steps—without fleeing, rushing, or bracing—and settles quietly when the cue releases.

intermediate.overview: Smooth, rhythmic, coordinated hindquarter yielding in both directions from halt or active walk with minimal unwanted drift, calm adaptability across practical spaces, and relaxed pause on release.

components.title: Balance from walk or halt
components.description: Shifting smoothly between straight forward walk and coordinated hindquarter yielding without dropping heavily onto the forehand or stepping backward unintentionally.

components.title: Adaptability and light responsiveness
components.description: Answering light ground requests calmly in busier settings, doorways, gates, or tight maneuvering areas.

intermediate.learning: Connects walk and fuller hindquarter turns in both directions with intermittent forward/backward drift, uneven crossing rhythm, or mild tension around distractions.
intermediate.proficient: Smoothly and reliably yields its hindquarters around steadier shoulders from halt or walk in both directions on light ground cues, maintaining balanced rhythm, minimal unwanted drift, and relaxed attentiveness across everyday and busier settings.

exercises.title: Soft Crossing Steps Around Steadier Shoulders
exercises.summary: From a settled halt on flat footing, invite the horse to shift weight gently and step its inside hind leg cleanly underneath and across in response to light ground cues, then relax promptly into a brief pause on release.
exercises.whatToNotice: Watch for a rhythmic crossing step with relaxed ears and soft jaw rather than swinging the hips rapidly out of worry or stepping backward.

exercises.title: Smooth Hindquarter Control From Walk and Tighter Spaces
exercises.summary: From an active four-beat walk on both sides, encourage smooth, rhythmic crossing steps around balanced shoulders with minimal forward drift, pausing settled whenever pressure drops.
exercises.whatToNotice: Check whether both left and right hips cross with similar ease and looseness—one-sided stiffness highlights where extra patience or physical checks help.

commonDifficulties.issue: Flinging the hindquarters fast or kicking out defensively
commonDifficulties.guidance: Sharp movement usually means cues felt startling or too intense. Soften energy, reward the earliest gentle weight shift, and let breathing stay slow.

commonDifficulties.issue: Stepping forward in a circle instead of crossing behind
commonDifficulties.guidance: Forward drifting means the shoulders stayed moving. Reset smoothly from a brief halt and ask for just one clear crossing step at a time.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: When a horse understands yielding the hindquarters smoothly, it builds physical suppleness and an easy way to release tension.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Distinguish genuine comprehension from anxious spinning or shutdown, work on non-slip ground, and check hock, stifle, hip, or back comfort if one direction consistently resists.

subject: horse
name: Yielding the Forequarters (In-Hand)
summary: The horse's calm comprehension and coordinated shoulder crossing when asked from the ground to step its forequarters aside around steadier hindquarters without crowding or rushing backward.
purpose: Develops respectful shoulder boundaries, forehand lightness, and balanced spatial responsiveness for trailer/gate alignment and mounted shoulder control.
safety: Distinguish calm understanding from head-tossing, running backward in worry, or crowding forward into personal space.
Investigate shoulder, neck, hoof, or knee discomfort if a horse consistently stiffens or resists stepping aside in one direction.

introductory.overview: From halt or quiet walk, calmly understanding light ground requests to step the shoulders aside in both directions without throwing the head defensively, backing abruptly, or crowding forward, and pausing softly on release.

components.title: Confidence with shoulder requests
components.description: Accepting cues near the head, neck, and shoulder calmly without feeling trapped or bolting backward.

components.title: Clean front stepping and boundary respect
components.description: Stepping the front feet cleanly across/around while respecting handler space and settling promptly on release.

introductory.learning: Steps shoulders aside in familiar spaces with occasional backward steps, raised neck tension, crowding toward the handler, or hesitation on the stiffer side.
introductory.proficient: Calmly understands light ground requests to step its shoulders aside in both directions with relaxed head and neck posture, polite space respect, and settled pauses on release—without rushing backward or crowding.

intermediate.overview: Coordinated, balanced shoulder yielding around relatively steady hindquarters in both directions from halt or walk on light requests—staying relaxed, avoiding unwanted backing, and adapting calmly in varied spaces.

components.title: Coordinated balance over steady hindquarters
components.description: Allowing the hind legs to pivot comfortably without twisting abruptly on a stuck limb or stepping steadily backward while shoulders cross smoothly.

components.title: Walk-to-yield flow and composure
components.description: Responding softly to shoulder redirection during leading, gate positioning, or busier settings.

intermediate.learning: Performs fuller forequarter yields and walk redirections in both directions with intermittent backward drift, rushed front steps, or uneven bend.
intermediate.proficient: Smoothly and reliably yields its forequarters around relatively steady hindquarters from halt or walk in both directions on light ground requests, maintaining balanced foreleg crossing, relaxed posture, and adaptability in varied settings without unintended backing.

exercises.title: Measured Shoulder Crossing Without Backing
exercises.summary: From a settled halt on even ground, encourage the horse to shift weight slightly off the forehand and cross its front legs smoothly sideways away from light ground cues for one or two steps, settling softly as soon as cues drop.
exercises.whatToNotice: Look for relaxed poll carriage and clean front-leg crossing around steadier hindquarters rather than tossing the head up or scuttling backward.

exercises.title: Balanced Multi-Step Shoulder Turns Both Sides
exercises.summary: From halt or slow walk on both left and right sides, build several balanced forequarter steps around steadier hind feet with light, consistent rhythm and soft pauses on release.
exercises.whatToNotice: Observe whether the horse steps freely across the chest in both directions without crowding forward or pinning ears.

commonDifficulties.issue: Backing up abruptly when asked to move the shoulders
commonDifficulties.guidance: Backing indicates the horse feels crowded in front. Keep the line light and ask gently beside the shoulder rather than pushing backward at the nose.

commonDifficulties.issue: Stiffening one shoulder and leaning into the handler
commonDifficulties.guidance: Natural asymmetry or soreness can make one direction harder. Ask for a single small try, praise softly, and check front hoof, knee, or shoulder comfort if stiffness persists.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: Light shoulder yielding teaches the horse to carry weight back onto its hindquarters rather than falling onto its front end.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Avoid forcing rapid turns on slick footing and investigate persistent one-sided shoulder stiffness, head tossing, or resistance for front-limb or neck discomfort.

subject: horse
name: Lateral Yielding / Sidepass (In-Hand)
summary: The horse's calm comprehension and balanced full-body coordination when stepping sideways from the ground with shoulders and hindquarters moving evenly together.
purpose: Integrates front- and hind-end ground communication into smooth, parallel sideways movement for gates, mounting blocks, tight spaces, and future mounted lateral balance.
safety: Introduce sideways coordination on open, level, non-slip ground—allow small relaxed tries without continuous squeezing or trapping.
Do not add obstacles or rails before the horse understands light sideways cues calmly in open space; assess back, rib, hoof, or limb soreness if chronic unevenness or tension appears.

introductory.overview: Calmly understanding light ground cues on open ground to coordinate both shoulders and hindquarters sideways in both directions with developing straightness, remaining relaxed without fleeing or rushing forward/backward, and pausing quietly on release.

components.title: Understanding combined sideways requests
components.description: Translating light ground requests into calm sideways steps rather than whipping the hips around or escaping forward or backward.

components.title: Developing alignment and emotional composure
components.description: Beginning to move front and hind ends together with soft breathing and settling peacefully when released.

introductory.learning: Attempts sideways steps on open ground with shoulders or hindquarters lagging, occasional forward or backward drifting, hurried steps, or mild tension between sides.
introductory.proficient: Calmly understands light ground cues on open, flat ground to step both front and hind ends sideways in both directions with unhurried composure, developing straightness, and a relaxed pause when released—without fleeing, crowding, or rushing.

intermediate.overview: Reliable, coordinated, balanced sideways stepping in both directions with shoulders and hindquarters staying largely parallel on light cues, calmly adaptable across everyday practical contexts (such as gates, mounting areas, or optional ground rails).

components.title: Even, parallel lateral coordination
components.description: Crossing both front and hind pairs rhythmically sideways in both directions with minimal shoulder or hip lag and minimal unwanted forward/backward drift.

components.title: Adaptability in practical contexts
components.description: Applying light sideways positioning calmly near barn doors, mounting areas, trail gates, or optional ground poles without pawing, rushing, or losing composure.

intermediate.learning: Moves sideways in both directions with intermittent unevenness between front and hind crossing, minor forward or backward drift, or distraction around gates, mounting blocks, or rails.
intermediate.proficient: Smoothly and reliably steps sideways in both directions on light ground cues with front and hind quarters staying calmly parallel and coordinated, maintaining steady unhurried rhythm and composure across varied practical contexts.

exercises.title: Coordinated First Sideways Steps on Open Ground
exercises.summary: On flat, non-slip ground—using a fence smoothly ahead if helpful—invite the horse to organize shoulders and hindquarters together for one or two relaxed sideways steps in each direction, pausing promptly as soon as both ends respond.
exercises.whatToNotice: Look for steady breathing and even crossing of front and hind legs rather than rushing sideways, hollowing the back, or trailing the hips far behind.

exercises.title: Parallel Sideways Steps for Gates and Everyday Spaces
exercises.summary: Develop several parallel sideways steps in open space on both sides, applying that poised coordination beside gates, mounting blocks, or an optional stable ground rail once open steps stay relaxed.
exercises.whatToNotice: Check whether the horse keeps a soft back and steady tempo across both directions without speeding up to escape the request.

commonDifficulties.issue: Crossing one end while the other stays planted
commonDifficulties.guidance: Full-body lateral coordination takes mental processing. Break practice back into brief alternating hindquarter and forequarter steps, then reconnect smoothly for one unified step.

commonDifficulties.issue: Hurrying sideways with a high tense head
commonDifficulties.guidance: Speed signals worry or over-cueing. Ask for a single slow step, let the horse stand and breathe, and avoid adding ground poles until open steps feel easy.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: Even sideways stepping grows from clarity and body awareness—one balanced step beats six frantic ones.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Keep sessions short on sound footing and evaluate chronic one-sided resistance, tripping, or back tension for hoof, limb, rib, or back soreness.
